studies.label: Argumentative writing experiment; randomized Phase 1 and separately recruited, nonrandom Phase 2

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 26, Table 3, Sample Size row; column order: Engage-to-Unlock, Standard Chatbot, Human-Only, Time-Matched Unlock, Total. PDF p. 6, section 3.2 confirms these are analyzed counts.

arms.name: Human-Only
arms.description: Randomized Phase 1; wrote with shared readings and without the assistant.

arms.name: Standard Chatbot
arms.description: Randomized Phase 1; Tell-me direct generative writing assistance available throughout.

arms.name: Engage-to-Unlock
arms.description: Randomized Phase 1; Teach-me guidance available throughout; Tell-me became available after a position and a distinct supporting argumentative development were detected in the draft. Unlocking did not automatically change modes.

arms.name: Time-Matched Unlock
arms.description: Nonrandom Phase 2, retained here only to describe the complete reported sample. Separately recruited participants received a prior Engage-to-Unlock participant unlock schedule. All contrasts involving this arm are excluded.

studies.country: Canada; India; South Africa; United Kingdom; United States
studies.task: Write an argumentative essay of at least 200 words about the four-day workweek using four source summaries; the writing task qualifies through its across-writer semantic-dispersion outcome (PDF p. 7, section 3.3; PDF pp. 9 and 13).

ai_tool.name: gemini-3.1-pro-preview
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 5, section 3.1, Assistant Modes; PDF pp. 26-29, Appendix D. The model release year is not stated.

preregistration.where: No preregistration identified in the complete article or included appendices. Planned contrasts are described in PDF p. 8, section 3.5.1.

estimates.outcome: Within-condition semantic dispersion of final essays (D_c)
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Mean squared Euclidean distance of complete essay embeddings from their own condition centroid. Gemini Embedding 2, SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY, 3,072 dimensions; whitespace normalized. One condition-level dispersion statistic per set of writers (PDF p. 9, section 3.5.3).

sources.locator: PDF p. 13, Table 1, Standard Chatbot row
PDF p. 13, Table 1, Human-Only row
PDF p. 13, Table 1 caption
sources.quote: with brackets reporting 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals (5,000 resamples).

estimates.notes: The CI fields contain only the treatment-arm interval, not an interval for the arm difference. Control-arm 95% percentile-bootstrap CI: [0.167, 0.188], preserved from its Table 1 source row. Printed homogenization indices relative to Human-Only: Standard Chatbot -0.050 (-5.0%); Human-Only 0.000 (baseline). HI_c is the same dispersion outcome transformed as 1 - D_c/D_Human-Only; higher HI_c means more similarity, opposite to higher D_c. HI_c is retained here rather than entered as a standardized effect with the wrong direction. The paper uses 5,000 bootstrap resamples but does not specify the resampling unit or provide a difference SE, difference CI, or formal between-condition test (PDF p. 9). n_units is null because the paper does not print the number of sets specifically for this two-arm contrast. Arm levels support a descriptive full-sample comparison.

estimates.outcome: Normalized content-word frequency profiles of final essays
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Content-word frequencies per 1,000 essay words, averaged across essays for the 85 most frequent content words in Human-Only. Lowercasing and alphabetic tokenization exclude single-character tokens and closed-class stopwords. Figure 7 shows means and SEM bands (PDF pp. 9 and 28).

sources.locator: PDF p. 6, section 3.2, analyzed arm counts

sources.locator: PDF p. 28, Appendix C, Figure 7 caption
sources.quote: Figure 7 | Mean normalized frequencies (occurrences per 1,000 words) of the 85 most frequent content words in Human-Only, ordered by descending Human-Only frequency. Points show condition means across essays and shaded bands indicate ±1 SEM.

estimates.notes: Higher values mean more occurrences of a particular content word per unit of essay length; no scalar creativity or diversity direction applies. Every numerical outcome field is null because the figure supplies unlabeled curves, points, and SEM bands without a numeric token-level table. No values were read off the figure, and no profile-average score was invented. SEMs are described as across essays, with one final essay per participant. The profile is retained as one descriptive outcome per arm comparison. The current text_features code is used for normalized content-word counts; the earlier screening form lacked a matching vocabulary code.

open_items: Assignment-stage totals, per-arm randomized counts, phase-specific counts before exclusion, and arm-specific attention-check exclusions are not printed. The reported 445 counts session completers, and 398 counts analyzed people across both phases (PDF p. 6). The randomized-phase total and two-arm totals are left null rather than calculated.

Semantic dispersion has arm-level percentile-bootstrap intervals but no difference SE, difference CI, or formal contrast test. The bootstrap resampling unit and procedure are not specified (PDF pp. 9 and 13). Control-arm intervals are preserved in notes and source rows because the provided schema has only one CI triplet.

Most discourse outcomes lack arm SDs, differences, SEs, test statistics, degrees of freedom, and intervals, despite the methods promising them. Category count and density have only a general nonsignificance statement; counterclaim count has only a pairwise p-value (PDF pp. 8 and 15; appendices checked).

PC1 has printed participant-arm centroids but no arm SDs or numerical contrast SE. PC2 and PC3 have no printed participant-arm means or numerical planned-contrast tests (PDF pp. 12 and 14). Figure ellipses are not transcribed as numerical uncertainty.
Content-word frequency means and SEMs are figure-only, with no printed token-level values; no numerical values were read from Figure 7 (PDF p. 28).
The standardizing SD for the printed AI-text coverage d is not defined (PDF p. 13, section 4.1.2).
The assistance model release year and the separate discourse-classifier model name are not stated (PDF pp. 5-6 and 26).
Preregistration, a public data/code repository, and a separate external supplement are not identified in the article or included appendices.
notes: Extraction B independently checked the complete markdown, including references and Appendices A-E, and used PyMuPDF text for the PDF tables, figures, design, methods, and every cited numerical result. The manuscript and PDF page numbers coincide. No outside source or other extractor file was used. One study describes the complete two-phase experiment: study n_analyzed includes the separately recruited Time-Matched Unlock cohort, but online_rct classification and every estimate apply only to Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, and Engage-to-Unlock. No randomized-phase or two-arm total was computed. All numeric n_treatment and n_control fields count analyzed people, never essays, ratings, or the AI-only corpus. AI role other denotes the combination of coach-style Teach-me and direct-generative Tell-me assistance; both use the same named model (PDF pp. 5-6 and 26-29). Cross-paper sample overlap is not stated; Phase 2 excluded Phase 1 participants, and the PERSUADE validation corpus is separate (PDF p. 6). All retained output measures concern the final Task 1 essays. Availability includes Teach-me guidance before or without a Tell-me unlock. No after_ai creative-production outcome is reported. Reported descriptive arm summaries and profiles support all eligible arm pairs; they are not labeled as formally tested effects. Only Engage-to-Unlock versus Standard Chatbot is a planned randomized inferential contrast (PDF p. 8). Null-valued category, density, remaining-PCA, and lexical-profile records preserve reported output contrasts with missing numbers. Semantic dispersion is the across_people outcome. PCA location, rhetorical structure, and source/AI borrowing are other constructs, not validated creativity, idea fluency, or cross-person diversity. Length uses the current length measure; normalized word counts use text_features. Higher_is other is explained in each record, with no inferred creativity valence. All printed percentages remain percentages. No effects, differences, SDs, SEs, intervals, event counts, or participant totals were computed. Numeric JSON values do not retain trailing zero formatting; the verbatim source quotes preserve the printed precision and signs. Inventory of in-scope numerical reporting: Table 1 (PDF p. 13) supplies each randomized arm dispersion, its 95% percentile-bootstrap CI, and HI_c; the HI_c transformation and control-arm CIs are preserved in estimate notes/source rows. Section 4.2.3 (PDF p. 14) supplies essay means, SDs, and medians; Table 2 (PDF p. 15) repeats rounded means/SDs and supplies source-coverage means/SDs, source-match percentages, AI-coverage means/SDs, and AI-match percentages. Section 4.2.4 (PDF p. 15) supplies discourse-element means and the counterclaim planned p-value; other discourse contrasts are narrative only. Section 4.2.1 (PDF p. 14) supplies PC1 arm centroids and its planned p-value; remaining component contrasts are narrative only. Section 4.1.2 (PDF p. 13) supplies the AI-coverage planned p-value and d. Figure 7 (PDF p. 28) supplies no printed token-level means or SEMs. Other printed statistics on these outcomes are omnibus, not eligible two-arm test results: essay length Welch F(3, 216.55) = 1.43, p = .234, omega-squared = .004, eta-squared = .012 (PDF p. 15); total discourse elements F(3, 394) = 4.66, p = .003 (PDF p. 15). Figure 2 (PDF p. 12) reports five-corpus PCA: PC1 explains 17.91%, F(4, 493) = 255.62, p < .001; PC2 explains 4.44%, F(4, 493) = 0.56, p = .693; PC3 explains 3.61%, F(4, 493) = 13.59, p < .001. These omnibus statistics are kept in this inventory and excluded from each pairwise stats object. The same dispersion outcome is not duplicated as a separate homogenization outcome; component-specific PCA contrasts are separated because their scores differ.
